analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime for companies to hide serious product or workplace dangers.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in October 2015 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it a federal crime, punishable by up to five years in prison, for a company or its executives to knowingly sit on information about a serious danger — a product defect or business practice with an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Companies would have had to notify a federal agency within 24 hours, warn affected workers and identifiable members of the public, and could not retaliate against employees who reported dangers. The measure died in committee without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and workers who would learn sooner about dangers hiding in products, services, or workplace practices; and whistleblowing employees, who would gain a federal right to sue for reinstatement, back pay, and damages if fired or punished for warning others.

how_it_helps.text: After learning of a serious danger, a company and its responsible executives would have had to verbally notify a federal agency within 24 hours, follow up in writing within 15 days, and warn exposed employees and identifiable members of the public, on penalty of a fine and up to five years in prison [S3].
Executives could not have company assets pay their fines, so the penalty would come out of the officer's own pocket [S3].

Employees who reported dangers could not be made to sign away these rights through arbitration agreements, and could recover reinstatement, back pay, and attorney's fees through the Labor Department or federal court [S3].

The bill responded to repeated cases of companies concealing known hazards — concealed dangers that are not readily apparent to a reasonable person, creating an imminent risk of death or serious injury [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Business entities and their executives, who would face criminal liability and mandatory rapid disclosure whenever they learn of a serious danger, plus the cost of warning workers and the public.

drawbacks.text: The trigger is broad: any executive with responsibility for knowing about a danger could face up to five years in prison for a knowing failure to report, and the definitions of 'serious danger' and 'responsible corporate officer' would leave companies navigating significant legal uncertainty about what must be reported and who is on the hook [S3].

The 24-hour verbal reporting deadline and 'as soon as practicable' warning requirements could push companies toward defensive, premature over-reporting of unverified hazards, flooding agencies and alarming the public before facts are established [S3].
Criminal exposure on top of existing civil and regulatory liability could raise compliance costs that businesses pass along in prices, a trade-off supporters accepted as the price of safety [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a narrow, serious harm — knowingly concealing an imminent risk of death or serious injury — so the burden falls mainly on companies that would otherwise have an incentive to stay quiet. The main costs are compliance burdens and legal uncertainty for executives, which honest supporters would weigh against the lives and injuries that faster disclosure could prevent.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat for the remaining fifteen months of the Congress with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Blumenthal, joined by Sen. Robert Casey, introduced the bill on October 6, 2015, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary [S1] [S3] [S5].
The complete action history contains only those two entries: introduction and referral. The Judiciary Committee took no further action, and the bill never reached the Senate floor [S5].
With only one cosponsor and no committee action, the bill expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1] [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies and their executives are better off because the bill died: they face no new criminal duty to disclose serious dangers and no new federal whistleblower protections. Consumers and workers gain nothing.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to criminalize concealing serious product and workplace dangers.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the remaining fifteen months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no opposition is recorded in the congressional record; the bill simply stalled in committee with two Democratic sponsors and no other cosponsors.

industries.industry: Consumer product manufacturers and service companies
industries.note: The bill would have imposed criminal liability for concealing serious dangers and required rapid disclosure to agencies, workers, and the public. Its defeat preserves the status quo in which companies face no federal criminal penalty for staying silent about known imminent hazards.

Responsible officers would have faced up to five years in prison personally, with company assets barred from paying their fines. Their interest in avoiding personal criminal exposure runs against the public's interest in prompt warnings.
The bill would have barred predispute arbitration agreements for whistleblower retaliation claims, giving employees court access they can currently be required to sign away.
